title: Large-reservoir storage that passes sediment without giving up carryover water

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a structure or operating method that moves incoming river sediment through a large, deep reservoir while retaining the water stored across multiple years and the normal operating head needed for water supply or hydropower. Carryover water is the reserve held for later dry seasons or drought years. The goal is to maintain that reserve while allowing sediment to continue downstream, rather than accumulating in the storage pool.

Scope synthesis: success requires sediment passage and retained reservoir services together. Removing sediment while substantially emptying a small irrigation tank would not demonstrate this capability. Flushing, sluicing, dredging and bypass tunnels are relevant approaches to examine, but the supplied evidence does not establish how broadly they already satisfy the combined requirements for deep reservoirs with multi-year storage. The concept is therefore a defined engineering target whose present availability remains unresolved.

significance.text: Reservoir sedimentation threatens the storage on which water supply, irrigation and hydropower depend. Liu, Fan, Song and coauthors’ 2026 assessment identifies sedimentation hotspots threatening water supplies to more than 2 billion people and affecting approximately 26% of global irrigated land. These are exposure estimates from an assessment, rather than evidence that all those services have already been lost.

Conditional significance synthesis: a broadly applicable method that passes sediment while retaining carryover water and operating head could substantially extend reservoir service life without sacrificing the services that make deep storage valuable. Its potentially revolutionary contribution is the simultaneous preservation of water storage and sediment movement. Passing a majority of the incoming load, however, could still leave substantial deposition; it would not by itself make a reservoir a permanent asset.

Conditional downstream synthesis: successful passage would deliver sediment below the dam. Benefits farther downstream, including replenishment of deltas, would depend on subsequent transport, intervening barriers, sediment characteristics and river management. The supplied material does not establish those outcomes. Sediment continuity is one component of river and delta management; it does not by itself provide protection against sea-level rise, storm surge, tsunami or earthquake.

Scope synthesis: reducing sediment entering a reservoir and moving sediment through it address different parts of the problem. Even if watershed erosion control reduces future inflow, that alone would not remove deposits already trapped or demonstrate sediment continuity through a full storage pool. The supplied evidence does not quantify the effectiveness of watershed measures for this target.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to establish is sustained sediment passage through a large, deep reservoir while carryover water, usable storage and normal operating head remain available. The global assessment documents the sedimentation problem and a need for management. Its supplementary material lists flushing and mechanical dredging examples and costs, but does not establish their compatibility or incompatibility with these combined requirements. The evidence therefore leaves open whether the advance requires a new technology, a new combination of existing methods, or broader deployment of capabilities already demonstrated elsewhere.

Engineering synthesis: the central difficulty is moving sediment through or around a deep storage pool without using prolonged drawdown to provide the necessary transport conditions. A practical design must account for where sediment settles, how it reaches a passage route, how different particle sizes behave and how much water or energy transport consumes. These are requirements inferred from the target, not performance limitations demonstrated for every existing method by the supplied sources.

Engineering synthesis: additional barriers include integrating passages or sediment-removal equipment with existing dam structures, maintaining operation during sediment-rich floods, controlling blockage and abrasion, and coordinating sediment releases with downstream conditions. The long-term challenge is a sediment balance: residual deposition must remain compatible with the intended storage life. Site geometry, flood timing and operating obligations could constrain transfer from a successful installation to other reservoirs.

current_state.text: Published online on 5 June 2026, Liu, Fan, Song and coauthors’ “Global patterns of reservoir sedimentation and overlooked risks in small reservoirs” is an inventory and physics-guided machine-learning assessment with projections. It is not a demonstration of sediment passage with retained carryover storage and head. Its supplementary table covers 555,960 reservoirs. The reported estimates should not be read as direct sedimentation measurements at every reservoir.

The abstract reports a global average reservoir storage loss of 7.3% ± 2.8% per decade. Supplementary Table 2 separately reports an annual sedimentation rate of 0.73% and an annual aggregate capacity loss rate of 0.48%. The reservoir-average rate and aggregate capacity loss describe different metrics; the decadal average should not be presented as an equivalent percentage loss of total global storage capacity.

Without intervention, the authors project that more than half of reservoirs could become functionally inoperable by 2060, including 58.6% of small reservoirs and 38.1% of large reservoirs. These are conditional projections whose meaning depends strongly on the definition of functional loss. An inspected extended-data caption reports 24.5% non-functional reservoirs under a 75% sedimentation threshold and 7.9% under a 100% threshold. These are alternative definitions, not contradictory forecasts. The threshold underlying the headline projection was not established in the supplied accessible main-article text.

The supplied review had access to a subscription preview containing the abstract, author information and ancillary material, plus the complete extracted text of a substantive supplement covering methods and tables. The full main article remained subscription-limited, and the supplement’s figure images were not inspected. A second PDF yielded essentially blank extracted pages with an extraction warning; its identity and contents were not confirmed by the review, so it contributes no verified substantive evidence here.

The inspected supplementary text documents modeling work and includes examples of flushing and mechanical dredging, rather than a demonstrated installation meeting this concept’s combined requirements. Neither that finding nor the absence of such a demonstration in the abstract proves that no qualifying method exists elsewhere. The supplied search record is empty, so the field’s status through 1 November 2026 remains unverified.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a method or structure at at least one large, deep reservoir with multi-year storage over several flood seasons, passing a measured majority of incoming sediment while carryover water, active storage and normal operating head remain available for water supply or power. Define reservoir scale and depth, monitoring duration, the majority threshold and allowable service interruptions before testing. These are proposed criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurements: account for incoming sediment, sediment delivered downstream and sediment remaining in the reservoir, with stated measurement uncertainty. Reservoir surveys alone are insufficient because a change in surveyed volume does not directly establish downstream delivery. Resolve relevant differences among sediment sizes and track where residual deposits accumulate, so that passage performance can be connected to future usable storage rather than only a single total-load percentage.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed measurements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed service and practical checks: document water consumed or released for sediment management, changes in usable storage and head, interruptions to water supply or power, energy requirements, maintenance, blockage or abrasion, cost and downstream release conditions. A small tank emptied for flushing would not meet the intended scope. Temporary operating changes should be evaluated against predefined service limits rather than treated automatically as either success or failure.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed service and practical checks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and breadth: provide operating records, measurement methods and uncertainty analysis sufficient for independent assessment and repeated performance across flood seasons. Success at one reservoir would demonstrate the capability there. Evidence from additional reservoir geometries, sediment regimes and operating constraints would be needed to establish broader applicability. Longer monitoring and an explicit residual-deposition budget would be needed to support service-life claims; finite tests cannot establish literal universality or indefinite storage preservation.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and breadth

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CIV-06, “Underground routes and spaces at surface-infrastructure cost,” could overlap if sediment passage uses a bypass tunnel. CIV-06 concerns the cost of underground construction; CIV-08 concerns sediment transport while retaining reservoir services. Affordable tunneling could enable an implementation without establishing its hydraulic performance or sediment balance.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-02, “Mechanics-based prediction of earthquake liquefaction and its ground consequences,” and CIV-03, “In-place conversion of ordinary ground into a specified engineering solid,” could be relevant to foundations, deposited sediments or construction around a reservoir. Their targets are ground-behavior prediction and ground transformation, respectively. CIV-08 instead targets sediment movement through an operating storage system.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-01, “A primary structural binder at global cement scale without process carbon dioxide”; CIV-04, “Repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking”; CIV-05, “Tensile-ductile mineral structures that replace reinforced concrete at ordinary cost”; CIV-07, “Load-bearing engineered living materials for ordinary structures”; and CIV-11, “Default-cost reinforcement with carbon-steel behavior and no corrosion in ordinary exposures,” address structural materials and durability. Such advances might affect construction or maintenance of sediment-management infrastructure, but none inherently demonstrates sediment passage with retained carryover storage.

Roster-based synthesis: CIV-09, “Immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake, at life-safety cost,” and CIV-12, “Fail-safe adaptive primary structural response at ordinary-building cost,” share a broad concern with maintaining infrastructure service but address building performance. CIV-10, “Structural concrete that stores building-relevant energy,” concerns electrical energy storage in a material; CIV-08 concerns stored water and hydraulic head. These remain distinct capabilities despite their connections to resilience and energy services.

change_log.change: Preserved CIV-08 and its original title while defining the innovation as a combined sediment-passage, carryover-storage and operating-head capability.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent even though the supplied evidence does not establish its present availability.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims that existing flushing, sluicing, dredging and bypass methods cannot meet the target with an explicit evidence boundary.
change_log.reason: The reviewed material does not establish their field-wide capabilities or limitations for deep multi-year reservoirs.

change_log.change: Integrated the distinction between reservoir-average sedimentation and aggregate capacity loss, retaining the supported numerical rates.
change_log.reason: The reported 7.3% ± 2.8% decadal average and 0.48% annual aggregate capacity loss are different metrics.

change_log.change: Qualified the 2060 functionality projections with alternative sedimentation thresholds and the unresolved headline threshold.
change_log.reason: The inspected caption demonstrates sensitivity to the definition of functional loss.

change_log.change: Replaced permanent-asset and assured delta-restoration claims with conditional service-life and downstream benefits.
change_log.reason: Majority passage can leave continuing deposition, and delivery below a dam does not establish delivery to a delta.

change_log.change: Corrected the access description to include substantive supplementary text and preserved the uninspected-image and second-PDF extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: The earlier description understated available material, while successful file retrieval did not establish usable evidence from every artifact.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to include depth, carryover water, uncertainty, residual deposition, operational limits and independent assessment.
change_log.reason: These distinguish a meaningful reservoir-service demonstration from sediment removal alone and bound what one site can establish.

change_log.change: Added explicitly labeled engineering synthesis and roster comparisons without presenting them as findings of the assessment.
change_log.reason: The record needs concrete barriers and conceptual distinctions while keeping supplied evidence separate from inference.

unresolved_issues: Whether existing installations or operating methods already meet the combined sediment-passage, deep multi-year storage and normal-head requirements remains unverified.
The empty supplied search record cannot establish the state of the field through 1 November 2026.
The sedimentation threshold underlying the headline 2060 functional-inoperability projection was not established in the supplied accessible main-article text.
The full main article was unavailable to the review; supplementary figure images were not inspected, and the second PDF’s identity and substantive contents remain unconfirmed.
Reservoir size and depth, monitoring duration, allowable service interruptions and the proposed majority-passage threshold still require operational definitions.
Acceptable residual deposition, long-term storage preservation, practical costs and downstream consequences require site-specific evidence.
No review recommendation was rejected; qualifications that cannot be resolved from the supplied material remain explicit.
